taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO. Three accepted varieties are recognized globally; learner stays species-level. Field-key caution (2026-10-19): Kew/POWO currently accepts Phyla nodiflora, P. lanceolata and P. cuneifolia separately. Cardoso et al. (2025), Nordic Journal of Botany doi:10.1002/njb.04825, propose a broader P. nodiflora concept encompassing lanceolata and cuneifolia because leaf differences overlap. Retain the project's current Kew species concepts, but teach leaf traits as typical tendencies, not infallible single-character diagnoses.
look_here_first: Look at the leaf before the flower head. Frogfruit has opposite oblanceolate-to-elliptic leaves that are usually widest beyond the middle, with the teeth concentrated on the upper/distal half. Then confirm the creeping stems rooting at nodes and the dense cylindrical flower spike on a long axillary peduncle.

project_inclusion.range_basis: BONAP/NAPA maps Phyla nodiflora at county level and treats it as native in Texas. Hays County — UT Plant Resources Center's Purola Preserve flora lists P. nodiflora among plants occurring naturally and not introduced. Travis County — UT Plant Resources Center's Travis County Verbenaceae herbarium index includes P. nodiflora; additional wild Travis records are documented at Emma Long and Reimers Ranch. Williamson County — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed county treatment for P. nodiflora.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Frogfruit is widely planted as a groundcover. County proof uses native-flora/herbarium treatments, not landscape plantings.

best_field_traits: perennial clonal groundcover with prostrate to procumbent stems
creeping stems root at buried or contacting nodes
leaf blades oblanceolate to elliptic, commonly widest beyond the middle
leaf margins serrate mainly above the midpoint, often fewer than six teeth per side
single dense spherical-to-cylindrical flower spikes arise on axillary peduncles
tiny white to pink/purplish flowers open around the spike, often with yellow/orange/purple throats
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Phyla lanceolata: The best leaf split: P. nodiflora is usually widest beyond the middle and its teeth are concentrated in the distal half; P. lanceolata is widest nearer the middle and the teeth extend farther down the blade. Phyla cuneifolia: Wedgeleaf frogfruit has a more distinctly wedge-shaped leaf architecture. Use several mature leaves rather than one odd leaf, because Phyla leaf shape varies along a shoot. Glandularia spp.: Glandularia can also form low mats with verbena-like flowers, but its flowers are much larger and borne in more open terminal heads/spikes; Phyla has tiny flowers packed into a compact button/cylinder on a naked axillary peduncle.

comparisons.key_distinctions: The best leaf split: P. nodiflora is usually widest beyond the middle and its teeth are concentrated in the distal half; P. lanceolata is widest nearer the middle and the teeth extend farther down the blade. Wedgeleaf frogfruit has a more distinctly wedge-shaped leaf architecture. Use several mature leaves rather than one odd leaf, because Phyla leaf shape varies along a shoot. Glandularia can also form low mats with verbena-like flowers, but its flowers are much larger and borne in more open terminal heads/spikes; Phyla has tiny flowers packed into a compact button/cylinder on a naked axillary peduncle.
comparisons.taxonomy_caution: Kew recognizes P. lanceolata and P. cuneifolia separately (checked 2026-10-19), whereas a 2025 peer-reviewed revision proposes including both within P. nodiflora s.l. Use the following leaf comparison as a traditional practical field heuristic, not a definitive taxonomic test. When several leaves overlap strongly, record Phyla sp. pending additional evidence.

field_matrix.focus: Multiple mature leaves, flowering head, leaf base
field_matrix.usual_pattern: Oblanceolate or spoon-shaped blade often broadest above its midpoint; teeth typically near distal half; lower blade narrows to an untoothed wedge.
field_matrix.limitation: Shape and teeth vary markedly, including within a shoot.

field_matrix.focus: Multiple mature leaves at similar nodes
field_matrix.usual_pattern: Often more elliptic/lanceolate and broadest around the middle, with teeth usually extending farther down the blade.
field_matrix.limitation: Broad overlap with P. nodiflora; 2025 revision treats this name within P. nodiflora s.l.

field_matrix.usual_pattern: Traditionally distinguished by relatively wedge-shaped, thicker or more leathery foliage.
field_matrix.limitation: Leaf shape and texture can overlap; 2025 revision treats this name within P. nodiflora s.l.

field_matrix.focus: Where flower stalk starts; flower size and head arrangement
field_matrix.usual_pattern: Larger individual flowers in terminal heads/spikes rather than many tiny flowers in an axillary stalked button.
field_matrix.limitation: Low growth habit and pinkish/white flowers alone are not distinguishing.

visual_comparison.title: Frogfruit — trace the stalk, leaf edge, and tiny flower head
visual_comparison.subtitle: Real installed photos, with three arrows checked against the actual 1024×768 flower-head image. One documented photo is CC BY-NC and is included only for the standalone noncommercial educational learner.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: First see a creeping mat. Then find the axillary, nearly leafless flower stalk and the many tiny flowers; use SEVERAL leaves, not just one, to evaluate the frogfruit type.

items.label: 1 — Low mat and repeated heads
items.image_role: Field habit / leaves and flowering stalks
items.caption: Look for the low mat, opposite leaves, and several upright slender stalks holding small heads. Rooting at the nodes is typical, but actual roots are not visible clearly enough in this photo to label.
items.why_it_matters: Establishes field context; neither a creeping mat nor a buttonlike head by itself establishes which Phyla species it is.
items.creator: Dinesh Valke

items.label: 2 — Flower parts and leaf teeth (arrows)
items.image_role: Actual upper leaf teeth, tiny flowers, and leafless head stalk
items.caption: The upper portions of the leaves have conspicuous teeth while their narrowed bases tend to be entire. Many tiny individual flowers occupy a compact purplish head on a mostly leafless peduncle (flower stalk). The labels identify directly visible structures, not unphotographed roots or microscopic hairs.
items.why_it_matters: Together the leaf arrangement and small axillary head help establish Phyla. Leaf width and where teeth start only suggest traditional P. nodiflora versus P. lanceolata; they are not decisive when traits overlap.
items.creator: yating
items.photo_status: INSTALLED_EXACT_SPECIES; PHOTO_INSPECTED_2026-10-19; guide species #58 credits yating CC BY-NC; standalone NONCOMMERCIAL display only; original JPEG unchanged and live arrow overlay added

items.label: 3 — More mature leaves and heads
items.image_role: Several older serrate leaves and rounded-to-elongated heads
items.caption: Check multiple leaves along the mat: broad upper blades, toothed distal margins, and narrower bases. The flower head may elongate as it matures. This photo is a second independent growth view, not a microscopic hair or fruit confirmation.
items.why_it_matters: Leaf shape is variable; verifying the pattern on more than one leaf is better than diagnosing a plant from its most unusual leaf.
items.creator: Forest & Kim Starr
